problem: Source says 'but the difficulty was' (contrast with the majority rule just stated); the candidate drops the 'but'. Source 'an additional probability of a judicious choice' became 'a better chance', a comparative the source does not make.
replacement: It then remained only for them to choose the least dangerous of the various modes of election. The rules they laid down on this point correspond admirably to the safeguards the country’s physical and political constitution already provided. Their aim was to find the mode of election that would best express the people’s choice with the least possible excitement and suspense. First, it was agreed that a simple majority should decide, but the difficulty was to obtain this majority without the delay that it was most important to avoid. It rarely happens that one individual can immediately gather the majority of the votes of a great people. The difficulty is greater still in a republic of confederate States, where local influences tend to predominate. The means proposed to overcome this second obstacle was to delegate the nation’s electoral powers to a body of representatives. This mode of election made a majority more probable, for the fewer the electors, the greater the chance that they will reach a final decision. It also offered an added likelihood of a wise choice. It then remained to decide whether to entrust this right of election to a legislative body, the nation’s ordinary representative assembly, or to form an electoral assembly for the express purpose of nominating a President. The Americans chose the latter alternative. They believed that the individuals elected to make the laws were not fit to represent the nation’s wishes in electing its chief magistrate, and that, since they are chosen for more than a year, the constituency they represent might change its opinion in that time. They thought that if the legislature were empowered to elect the head of the executive power, its members would be exposed, for some time before the election, to the maneuvers of corruption and the tricks of intrigue. The special electors, by contrast, would remain mixed in with the crowd, like a jury, until the day of action, when they would appear for the sole purpose of casting their votes.

problem: 'recourse is had to the division of the States' rendered 'the States are divided', which reads as if the States themselves split; the sense is a vote divided by States.
replacement: w [ The electors of the same State assemble, but they transmit to the central government the list of their individual votes, and not the mere result of the vote of the majority.] [Footnote x: In this case it is the majority of the States, and not the majority of the members, that decides the question, so that New York has no more influence in the debate than Rhode Island. Thus the citizens of the Union are first consulted as members of one and the same community. If they cannot agree, recourse is had to a division by States, each of which has a separate and independent vote. This is one of the oddities of the Federal Constitution, and it can be explained only by the clash of conflicting interests.]

problem: Source: an interest 'assumes a great degree of importance as soon as it becomes general'. Candidate 'shared by everyone' overstates 'general'.
replacement: Nevertheless, the time of a presidential election in the United States may be considered a crisis in the affairs of the nation. The President’s influence on public business is no doubt weak and indirect. But the choice of President, which matters little to each individual citizen, concerns the citizens collectively, and however trifling an interest may be, it becomes very important as soon as it becomes general. Compared with the kings of Europe, the President has few means of rewarding his supporters. But the offices at his disposal are numerous enough to interest several thousand electors, directly or indirectly, in his success. Political parties in the United States are led to rally around an individual in order to take a more tangible shape in the eyes of the crowd, and the name of the candidate for the Presidency is held up as the symbol and personification of their theories. For these reasons parties have a strong interest in winning the election. They want less to see their principles triumph under the President-elect than to show, by the majority that elected him, how strong the supporters of those principles are.

problem: Footnote c left verbatim in 1862 wording (which-chains, 'entertained', capitalized 'central Government'); the footnote's own prose should be modernized and 'Government' lowercased.
replacement: c [ Federal laws are the ones that most need courts of justice, and at the same time the ones for which courts have most rarely been established. The reason is that confederations have usually been formed by independent States that had no real intention of obeying the central government, that very readily ceded the right of command to the federal executive, and that very prudently reserved the right of non-compliance for themselves.]

problem: 'inalienable' (office that cannot be taken away) rendered 'permanent', which loses the protection-from-removal sense.
replacement: The American legislators therefore agreed to create a federal judiciary to apply the laws of the Union and to decide certain questions affecting general interests, which were carefully defined in advance. The entire judicial power of the Union was concentrated in one tribunal, called the Supreme Court of the United States. But to speed the dispatch of business, inferior courts were attached to it. These were empowered to decide cases of small importance without appeal, and cases of greater magnitude with appeal. The members of the Supreme Court are named neither by the people nor by the legislature, but by the President of the United States, acting with the advice of the Senate. To make them independent of the other authorities, their office was made irremovable, and it was decided that once their salary was fixed, the legislature could not alter it. *d It was easy to proclaim the principle of a Federal judiciary, but difficulties multiplied when the extent of its jurisdiction had to be determined.
